title: Avalanche Buries Tent on Manaslu, Killing Indian-Origin Climber and Sherpa Guide
excerpt: Dhruba Jyoti Guha and guide Phursemba Sherpa pushed to Camp III for an early summit attempt while teammates retreated; their deaths take the mountain's autumn toll to four.
body:
• Indian-German climber Dhruba Jyoti Guha, 47, and his Nepali guide Phursemba Sherpa, 47, were found dead inside their tent at Camp III on Mount Manaslu on Sept. 20, buried under nearly seven feet of snow.
  • The pair had pushed from Camp II to Camp III on Saturday evening for an early summit attempt while six teammates retreated to safety; contact was lost overnight and four Sherpa climbers found the bodies around 11:30 a.m. Sunday.
  • Guha, a Bengal Engineering College graduate based near Frankfurt who worked at ABB, IBM, Pfizer and Nestlé, was an accomplished ultra-endurance trail runner; Sherpa had summited Everest nine times.
  • The deaths bring Manaslu's autumn toll to four, as heavy snowfall — up to 60 cm at base camp — forces hundreds of climbers to retreat or wait out the weather.

An Indian-origin climber and his Nepalese Sherpa guide were killed when an avalanche buried their tent at Camp III on Mount Manaslu, expedition organizers said Sunday, in the deadliest incident of an autumn season already marked by severe weather on the world's eighth-highest peak.

Dhruba Jyoti Guha, a 47-year-old Indian-German climber, and Phursemba Sherpa, a 47-year-old NMA-registered guide from Nepal's Makalu region, were found inside their tent at Camp III (around 6,800 meters) on the 8,163-meter mountain. Four Sherpa climbers dug through several feet of snow and ice to reach them after the pair stopped responding to communications, according to Mohan Lamsal, managing director of Makalu Adventure, the expedition organizer.

A fateful decision to push higher

Guha and Sherpa were part of a seven-member foreign climbing team. On Saturday evening, as conditions deteriorated, six of the climbers decided to retreat from Camp II. Guha and Sherpa instead moved up to Camp III to rest ahead of a planned early summit attempt, Lamsal told reporters, quoting fellow climbers.

"on Sunday after they stopped responding," Lamsal said."

Contact with the two was lost overnight. "We were alerted around 11:30 a.m. on Sunday after they stopped responding," Lamsal said. "We immediately sent four Sherpa climbers to Camp III to look for them. They dug through the snow and found both inside their tent, buried beneath nearly seven feet of snow."

Continuing snowfall and the risk of further avalanches prevented an immediate recovery. Lamsal said he ordered the rescue team to descend to lower camps for their own safety, adding that the bodies would be brought down once the weather improves. According to Firstpost, the bodies were later airlifted to Kathmandu.

Two accomplished mountaineers

Guha, based near Frankfurt in Germany, graduated in mechanical engineering from Bengal Engineering College, Shibpur (now IIEST Shibpur), in 2002, and went on to work with ABB, IBM, Pfizer and Nestlé. He was an accomplished ultra-endurance trail runner with 32 UTMB World Series race finishes, including several races over 100 kilometers.

Sherpa was among Nepal's most experienced high-altitude guides, with nine Everest summits to his name along with ascents of Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Cho Oyu and Manaslu.

A deadly season on Manaslu

With Sunday's casualties, Manaslu has recorded four deaths this autumn. On Sept. 17, Lau Wee Seng, a 50-year-old climber from Singapore, died at about 6,000 meters while descending from Camp II. On Sept. 5, Tashi Sherpa, a 20-year-old Nepali high-altitude worker, was found dead inside a tent at base camp.

Heavy snowfall began Friday evening and continued through Sunday, with up to 60 centimeters recorded at base camp, forcing hundreds of climbers to retreat to lower camps or remain in place. Veteran mountain meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar said the snowfall was associated with a western disturbance; forecasters are also monitoring a developing weather system in the Bay of Bengal that could alter conditions across South Asia between Sept. 23 and 25, though it is too early to say whether it will reach Nepal's high mountains.

The scale of the fatal slide has itself become a point of debate. Drone imagery taken Sunday afternoon appeared to show a relatively small area of disturbed snow above Camp III. "It was a small slab avalanche, but the media made it into bigger news," said veteran mountaineer Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, known as Mingma G, who was at base camp — a reminder that even modest slides are lethal at extreme altitude. A separate avalanche struck the same area on Sept. 16 as a rope-fixing team prepared for a summit push, forcing a retreat before the route was fixed on a later attempt.

What comes next

Expedition operators say a relatively favorable weather window from Sept. 21 to 23 has some climbers heading back to the high camps for summit attempts, while others wait out the Bay of Bengal system. For the families of Guha and Sherpa, the focus now turns to bringing the bodies home — Guha to a grieving community of Indian-origin mountaineers and trail runners in Europe and India, and Sherpa to the Makalu region that has supplied generations of Himalayan guides.
image_caption: Mount Manaslu in Nepal, where an avalanche buried a tent at Camp III, killing two climbers.
nri_angle: Guha was an Indian-origin engineer and ultra-runner based in Germany whose story resonates across the diaspora's growing adventure-sports community — a Bengal Engineering College graduate who carried his roots onto the world's highest peaks.
